name: Chonmage

lead: The chonmage is a Japanese men's topknot, historically worn by samurai and associated with the Edo period (1603-1868). Hair is gathered and tied up while the front scalp is shaved in the classic version.

It shapes the head outline, draws attention to the face and forehead, and carries cultural meaning of discipline and rank. Today it survives mainly in sumo, where wrestlers wear a modified version, and in kabuki.

paras: Traditionally the hair was oiled and tied by a specialist, and sumo wrestlers have their hair dressed by hairdressers called tokoyama. Modern topknot or man-bun styles borrow the shape without shaving the pate.

Constant tension from tight ties can strain the hair and hairline, and the shaved-pate form requires regular upkeep. The style is a strong cultural signal and may read differently outside its context.

angle.text: The style changes head shape and frames the face by pulling hair up and away. It is a deliberate cultural look rather than a mainstream cut.

lead: The chonmage is a traditional Japanese men's topknot, best known from the samurai of the Edo period.[1] In the classic form the top of the head (sakayaki) was shaved and the remaining hair tied up.[1]

Historians trace its roots to Heian-era aristocrats who tied hair to hold ceremonial caps; later it served helmet wear and became a mark of rank.[1][2] By the early Edo period samurai were required to shave the pate, while masterless ronin were not, which made them recognisable.[1]
The 1871 Dampatsurei Edict forced samurai to cut their hair, effectively ending the style. Today sumo wrestlers wear a modified version and kabuki actors also wear it.[1]

paras: The style varied with social rank, with samurai versions more pronounced than those of artisans or merchants.[1]

Early forms secured the kanmuri and eboshi headwear of nobles.[2] Later, samurai shaved the crown and tied a topknot, a form that also fit under helmets.[2] The Edo government required shaved pates for samurai, and by the 1660s all men were barred from wearing beards.[1]
The Meiji reforms modernised appearances in a Westernising nation, and the 1871 edict ended the style.[1]

Sumo wrestlers wear a modified chonmage in which the pate is not shaved but the hair may be thinned or the crown shaved (nakazori). Higher-ranked sekitori wear the elaborate oicho (ginkgo-leaf) style at tournaments. Cutting off the topknot is the centrepiece of a retirement ceremony.[1]

A 2026 editorial in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery compared Joseon-era topknot grooming with modern facial rejuvenation. It noted that the manggeon headband worn to secure the sangtu topknot compressed the temples and lifted the brows, an effect likened to modern brow-lift tension.[3]
No studies found on the chonmage itself. The editorial above is a historical comparison, not a trial.[3]
